    FAPD-AI: The First Circuit issued an opinion by Judge Dunlap in United States v. Newton, No. 25-1101, affirming the judgment of the District of Massachusetts. A jury convicted Faith Newton of one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud, one count of health care fraud, and three counts of money laundering, and the district court imposed a 144-month term of imprisonment. On appeal, Newton challenged the grant of self-representation at trial, the denial of suppression for cell phone data obtained by Customs and Border Protection at Boston Logan Airport, and the loss calculation and sophisticated means enhancement at sentencing, and the court stated that none of these arguments succeeded. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Linda Migliori, et al v. Lehigh County Board of Elections (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02761 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02761-0

    FAPD-AI: In this nonprecedential opinion, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed a district court's award of attorneys' fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988 to Linda Migliori and four other voter plaintiffs in their suit against the Lehigh County Board of Elections. The court held that the plaintiffs were a prevailing party, that the Board's objections met the specificity standard of Bell v. United Princeton Properties, Inc., that the district court's hours reduction and its Allentown market-rate determination were within its discretion and not clear error, and that fees for litigating the fee petition were properly denied because no lodestar analysis was submitted. Judge Matey, dissenting, would hold that the plaintiffs have no cause of action under 52 U.S.C. § 10101(a)(2)(B), would find that special circumstances preclude a fee award, and would vacate the judgment and remand. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 18:18:10 Eastern time ET
    In Re: Invitae Corporation, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02735 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02735-0

    FAPD-AI: This nonprecedential opinion, filed October 29, 2026, addresses the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors' appeal in the Invitae Corporation bankruptcy, which challenged the denial of its motion for derivative standing and the confirmation of Invitae's reorganization plan containing releases. The Third Circuit affirmed the district court's affirmance of the Bankruptcy Court's orders. It held that the Bankruptcy Court did not abuse its discretion in its cost-benefit analysis, which found that the costs of the Committee's proposed claims outweighed their likely benefits to the estate. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 18:18:09 Eastern time ET
    Linda Migliori, et al v. Lehigh County Board of Elections (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02650 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02650-0

    FAPD-AI: This nonprecedential opinion, filed October 29, 2026, addresses the Lehigh County Board of Elections' appeal and the plaintiff voters' cross-appeal, both arising from the district court's order granting in part and denying in part attorneys' fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988. The Third Circuit affirmed, finding the Board's objections sufficiently specific, the hour reduction within the district court's discretion, the Allentown rate determination free of clear error, and the denial of fees for the fee petition supported by the record. Judge Matey dissented, stating that the plaintiffs had no cause of action under 52 U.S.C. § 10101(a)(2)(B) and that fees should be denied or the judgment vacated. USCOURTS-SEL-01

      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-22-01499 / USCOURTS-ca3-22-01499-0

      FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit held that private plaintiffs may enforce the Materiality Provision of the Civil Rights Act, 52 U.S.C. § 10101(a)(2)(B), through an action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. It further held that Pennsylvania's requirements that mail-in ballot declarations be dated, 25 Pa. Cons. Stat. §§ 3146.6(a) and 3150.16, are immaterial to voter qualifications under that provision. The court reversed the district court's summary judgment for the Lehigh County Board of Elections and remanded with direction to count the undated ballots at issue. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Jackson v. Cornwell, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-26-05083 / USCOURTS-ca10-26-05083-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the Northern District of Oklahoma's dismissal of Tamar Jackson's pro se 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit against Derrick Yazel and Misty Cornwell, officials at the Northeast Oklahoma Community Correctional Center, which alleged denial of access to the courts and retaliation. The court held that Jackson could have handwritten his state-court motion, so he did not show the actual injury required for an access claim, and that he did not challenge the district court's retaliation, supervisory-liability, or official-capacity rulings. The order and judgment is nonbinding except as provided under the law of the case, res judicata, and collateral estoppel. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of a pro se plaintiff's § 1983 and New Mexico state-law claims against a private attorney and his law firm arising from a state domestic relations case.     Johnson v. Goodenow, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-26-03025 / USCOURTS-ca10-26-03025-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed in part the dismissal of a pro se plaintiff's § 1983 and Title II ADA claims arising from a Kansas state family-law proceeding, which named a state district judge, the state district court, its chief judge, and Johnson County. The court reversed the with-prejudice dismissal of claims dismissed for failure to state a claim, other than the ADA claim against Judge Goodenow in her individual capacity, and remanded with instructions to dismiss those claims without prejudice. The court stated that amendment of the ADA claim against the individual judge would be futile because only public entities are subject to Title II. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 18:18:00 Eastern time ET
    United States, et al v. FourPoint Resources (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-04121 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-04121-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of the Ute Indian Tribe's motion to intervene in a Clean Air Act enforcement action brought by the United States and Utah against Ovintiv's successor, FourPoint Resources. The district court had ruled that the Tribe lacked Article III standing to seek to set aside the consent decree, which required a $5,500,000 civil penalty and emissions mitigation, based on the United States' alleged failure to consult with the Tribe. The panel held that the Tribe did not show an injury in fact to its sovereign, quasi-sovereign, or economic interests, and it did not reach the United States' alternative grounds for affirmance. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-26-01042 / USCOURTS-ca10-26-01042-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit dismissed the appeal of a pro se prisoner whose § 1983 claims against officials at the Crowley County Correctional Facility were dismissed on screening under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i). The court held that his objections to the magistrate judge's report and recommendation were general and not sufficiently specific, so the issues were waived under the firm-waiver rule, and it found no basis to apply the interests-of-justice exception. The court granted the motion to proceed in forma pauperis and did not address whether the action was frivolous. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    California Chamber of Commerce, Et AL. V. Bonta, Et AL. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-6874 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-6874-0

    FAPD-AI: In California Chamber of Commerce v. Bonta, the Ninth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of California Senate Bill 399 (Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(c)), which prohibits employers from taking adverse action against employees who decline to attend employer-sponsored meetings or communications about religious or political matters. The panel held that the Western Growers Association had standing and that the industry groups were likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim, applying strict scrutiny and rejecting the captive audience justification for content-based restrictions on nongovernmental speech. The panel did not reach the preemption claim under the National Labor Relations Act. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:04:17 Eastern time ET
    Red Eagle Law, Lc V. Rubio (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-26-6943 / USCOURTS-ca9-26-6943-0

    FAPD-AI: In Red Eagle Law, L.C. v. Rubio, the Ninth Circuit granted the government's emergency motion for a stay pending appeal of a preliminary injunction that had required the State Department to reopen registration for the fiscal year 2027 Diversity Visa Program. The per curiam order held that the plaintiff law firm is not within the zone of interests of the Diversity Visa Program statute and does not have a cause of action, and it stated that the court does not endorse the Department's failure to open the registration period. Judge N. Randy Smith concurred, writing that the plaintiff also lacks Article III standing. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:04:16 Eastern time ET
    Maplebear INC., Et AL. V. City of Seattle (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-231 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-231-0

    FAPD-AI: In Maplebear Inc. (Instacart), et al. v. City of Seattle, the Ninth Circuit issued the same superseding amended opinion and dissent in this companion appeal (No. 25-231), consolidated with No. 25-228, affirming the denial of a preliminary injunction against Seattle's App-Based Worker Deactivation Rights Ordinance. The majority held that the ordinance's written-notice requirement meets the Zauderer test, that the 'reasonably related' requirement regulates speech concerning unlawful deactivations, and that the ordinance is not unconstitutionally vague. Judge Bennett dissented in part, stating that the ordinance compels speech and would vacate and remand. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Uber Technologies, INC., Et AL. V. City of Seattle (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-228 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-228-0

    FAPD-AI: In Uber Technologies, Inc. v. City of Seattle, the Ninth Circuit withdrew its March 4, 2026 opinion and issued a superseding amended opinion and dissent affirming the denial of a preliminary injunction against Seattle's App-Based Worker Deactivation Rights Ordinance. The majority held that the ordinance's requirement that network companies inform workers in writing of their deactivation policies meets the Zauderer test, that the 'reasonably related' requirement regulates speech concerning unlawful deactivations, and that the ordinance is not unconstitutionally vague. Judge Bennett dissented in part, stating that the ordinance compels speech and would vacate and remand for further proceedings. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:04:13 Eastern time ET
    Colvin and Son, Llc, Et AL. V. Burgum, Et AL. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-1888 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-1888-0

    FAPD-AI: In Colvin & Son, LLC v. Burgum, the Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for federal defendants in a challenge to two Bureau of Land Management gather plans for removing excess wild horses in Nye County, Nevada, covering the Little Fish Lake Joint Management Area and the Stone Cabin Complex. The panel held that the Wild Horses Act requires BLM to remove excess animals as promptly as logistically and reasonably possible, and that the Act does not require a specific time frame for removal actions. The panel concluded that the gather plans complied with the Act's immediacy requirement. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-03150 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-03150-0

    FAPD-AI: In this published opinion (File Name 26a0292p.06), the Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Cincinnati Bell Telephone Company, LLC, in a suit by Loren Bennink alleging unpaid overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act and breach of contract. The district court had found that Bennink was exempt from FLSA overtime requirements as a computer employee under 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(17) and that no contract existed between the parties. The appellate opinion addresses the scope of the computer employee exemption and the statutory language of § 213(a)(17)(B). USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: In this nonprecedential order (No. 25-3302), the Seventh Circuit denied Jaison Francisco's petition for review of a Commodity Futures Trading Commission final order.     Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-05766 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-05766-0

    FAPD-AI: In this published opinion (File Name 26a0293p.06), the Sixth Circuit affirmed the conviction of Alexander Miguel Laykovich under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(4), which prohibits firearm possession by a person adjudicated as a mental defective or committed to a mental institution. The court rejected Laykovich's facial Second Amendment challenge, holding that the provision has at least some constitutional applications. The court also rejected his challenges to the application of a straw-purchaser guidelines enhancement and to the 48-month sentence imposed by the district court. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-03210 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-03210-0

    FAPD-AI: In this opinion not recommended for publication, the Sixth Circuit affirmed the convictions of Joshua Fortson on federal drug-trafficking and firearm charges. Fortson challenged the denial of a pretrial continuance, the denial of a motion to suppress evidence from a warrantless parole search of an apartment, and the admission of post-arrest interview statements. The court found no abuse of discretion in the continuance ruling because Fortson did not show actual prejudice, and it found no reversible error in the remaining challenges. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-01899 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-01899-0

    FAPD-AI: In this opinion not recommended for publication, the Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's grant of qualified immunity to Otsego County, Michigan, and to the individual state and county officers named in Frances Collazo's Section 1983 suit. Collazo alleged that the officers used excessive force in arresting her for obstruction and resisting arrest after a 911 report of gunshots and shouting at her residence. The court concluded that the officers acted reasonably in a rapidly evolving situation and that qualified immunity applied even under Collazo's version of the facts. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: In an opinion dated October 29, 2026, authored by Circuit Judge Edith Hollan Jones, the Fifth Circuit reversed a district court order that adopted a magistrate judge's order granting Motorola's 28 U.S.C. § 1782 application for discovery of an unredacted patent purchase agreement from Advanced Standard Communication, L.L.C., for use in European patent proceedings. The court held that the district court should have reviewed the magistrate judge's order de novo as a dispositive matter, and that the district court misapplied the burden of proof and erred in weighing the Intel factors. Gibbs (No. 24-4150), affirmed a 204-month sentence imposed after a guilty plea to possession of a firearm and ammunition by a convicted felon, where the Armed Career Criminal Act mandatory minimum was 180 months and the advisory Guidelines range was 188-235 months. The court found that the district court did not base the sentence on a detective's testimony about a child's death, because the district court repeatedly stated it was not holding the defendant responsible for that death.       Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-60017 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-60017-1

      FAPD-AI: On remand from the Supreme Court, the Fifth Circuit issued an opinion dated October 29, 2026 in the appeal of Rashon Jermaine Harris, applying Hunter v. United States (2026), which holds that an appeal waiver is unenforceable when enforcing it would result in a miscarriage of justice. The court found that the appeal waiver was knowing and voluntary, that the same-day timing of the guilty plea did not undermine it, and that application of the U.S.S.G. § 3C1.2 enhancement did not constitute a miscarriage of justice, noting that standard-fare sentencing errors cannot cancel an appeal waiver. The court enforced the appeal waiver and dismissed the appeal. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated October 29, 2026, the Fifth Circuit addressed the appeal of Pedro Garcia Lopez, who was convicted and sentenced under the enhanced penalty provision of 8 U.S.C. § 1326(b)(2).     FAPD-AI: Public Law 119–68, approved December 29, 2025 as H.R. 1043 and cited as the La Paz County Solar Energy and Job Creation Act, directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey approximately 3,400 acres of Bureau of Land Management-managed federal land in La Paz County, Arizona, to the county upon its request. The conveyance is made at fair market value determined by appraisal, excludes lands containing significant cultural, environmental, wildlife, or recreational resources, and withdraws the land from the mining and mineral leasing laws. The county must pay the appraised value and conveyance costs, meet Tribal artifact protection conditions, and deposit sale proceeds in the Federal Land Disposal Account. PLAW-SEL-01

    119 HR 8183 RH: Modernizing Access to Talents, Credentials, and Hiring Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8183rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8183, the Modernizing Access to Talents, Credentials, and Hiring Act of 2026 (MATCH Act of 2026), was reported with amendments and would amend the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act to establish a pilot program of up to 5 years in which the Secretary of Labor awards grants to eligible entities for workforce longitudinal data systems and talent marketplaces. The bill sets grant application contents, priority criteria, grant durations of up to 3 years, and requirements for publicly available, consumer-tested websites that present program and talent marketplace information. It also requires reports to Congress, a Government Accountability Office evaluation after the pilot concludes, and the development of validated skills assessment tools in coordination with the Office of Personnel Management.     Federal Register · govinfo API · ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY · FR-2026-10-30 / 2026-22176

    official summary: This regulation establishes exemptions from the requirement of a tolerance for residues of dimethyl sulfoxide (CAS Reg. No. 67-68-5) when used as an inert ingredient (solvent/cosolvent) in pesticide formulations applied to growing crops or to raw agricultural commodities after harvest, in pesticide formulations applied to animals, and in antimicrobial formulations applied to food-contact surfaces in public eating places, dairy-processing equipment, and food-processing equipment and utensils. Spring Regulatory Sciences on behalf of Gaylord Chemical Company, LLC submitted a petition to EPA under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), requesting establishment of exemptions from the requirement of a tolerance. This regulation eliminates the need to establish maximum permissible levels for residues of dimethyl sulfoxide when used in accordance with the terms of those exemptions. FR-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 7254 would amend Section 5(c) of the National Trails System Act (16 U.S.C. 1244(c)) to add the Bay Area Ridge National Scenic Trail, described as a multi-use trail of approximately 550 miles along ridgelines around the San Francisco Bay Area. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to complete and submit to Congress a feasibility study for designating the trail within 3 years of enactment, in consultation with interested organizations including the Bay Area Ridge Trail Council and with each federal and state agency whose lands the trail crosses.   • Observed at 02:05:53 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 7954 RH: Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr7954rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 7954, the Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act, sets out congressional findings and purposes regarding buffalo management and reestablishment on Indian land. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to consult with Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations, to enter into contracts, cooperative agreements, and grants for buffalo restoration and management activities, and to provide technical assistance. The bill also requires protection of information identified by Tribes as culturally sensitive, proprietary, or confidential, authorizes the transfer of surplus buffalo from federal land to Tribes with possible waiver of charges, states that treaty rights are not altered, and sunsets the authority 7 years after enactment. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 02:05:53 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 8195 RH: Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8195rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8195, the Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026, directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Director of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, to issue regulations within 1 year of enactment for regional management frameworks governing the take of double-crested cormorants. Each framework must address allowable methods and time periods of take, annual public reporting of take, measures to avoid non-target birds, non-lethal measures, and authorized entities, among other requirements. The bill also requires population surveys and framework updates every 5 years, a report on the feasibility of issuing cormorant hunting licenses within 90 days of enactment, and provides that the Act has no force or effect beginning January 1, 2034. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 02:05:53 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 8483 RH: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8483rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8483, the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026, transfers administrative jurisdiction of approximately 683 acres of Forest Service land (Parcels 2 and 3) to the Secretary of the Interior and takes that land, together with approximately 164 acres of Bureau of Land Management land (Parcel 1), into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians. The land becomes part of the Tribe's reservation, subject to existing rights, Forest Service administrative vehicular access, continuing public recreational access, and emergency and fuels-management access. The bill prohibits class II and class III gaming on the transferred land, states that existing water rights are not altered, and requires the Tribe to maintain the fuel break in accordance with Forest Service standards. BILLS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 9785, the South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act, as reported with an amendment, directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct feasibility studies for three proposed Missouri River basin municipal, rural, and industrial water supply projects: the Western Dakota Regional Water System, the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System expansion, and the Dakota Mainstem Water Supply Project. For the first two studies, the Secretary must submit a feasibility report with a recommendation and a non-Federal cost share of at least 25 percent, and for the third study the Secretary may proceed through a cooperative agreement. For all three, the Federal share of study costs is capped at $10,000,000 and 50 percent of the total cost, and each study authority expires 7 years after enactment. BILLS-SEL-01

Reynolds Research Natural Area, and associated facilities to the State of Arkansas by quitclaim deed without consideration, if the State submits a written request within 180 days of enactment. The State must pay conveyance costs, designate the land as the Crossett Experimental State Forest, and use it for forest research, education, and demonstration in coordination with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture. If the State fails to meet these conditions and does not correct the failure within 180 days after written notice, the Secretary may revert the land to the United States, and the Forest Service must provide the State with copies of related research records.     Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr3331rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 3331, the Mariner Exam Modernization Act, amends Section 7510 of title 46, United States Code, concerning merchant mariner credential examination working groups. The bill adds required members to the working group, including individuals who passed the examination within the prior five years and a representative of the United States Merchant Marine Academy, and requires the Commandant to convene the group annually or when new questions are created. It also requires a review of the examination within 270 days, a plan to update and modernize the examination within 270 days after that review, a prohibition on using new questions until the working group approves them, and a Coast Guard briefing to congressional committees within one year of enactment. BILLS-SEL-01

It also amends Section 509(c)(1) of the Claims Resolution Act of 2010 for the Taos Pueblo Water Development Fund and Section 617(c)(1) of that Act for the Aamodt Settlement Pueblos' Fund to authorize comparable adjusted interest amounts, and directs the Secretary of the Treasury to waive certain amounts due on Aamodt-related interest earned before September 15, 2017. The bill includes disclaimers stating that it does not affect the prior satisfaction of specified conditions precedent or the Secretarial findings published in the Federal Register on October 7, 2016 and September 15, 2017, and it authorizes appropriation of investment earnings credited to the trust funds.     Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s675rh

    FAPD-AI: S. 675, the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Act, authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to provide grants of up to $50,000,000 to the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Foundation for establishing the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora, North Dakota, subject to appropriations. Grants may not be provided until the Foundation certifies it has received at least $100,000,000 from State of North Dakota funds or non-Federal sources, and grant funds may not be used for the library's maintenance or operation. The Act also authorizes the Secretary, within 180 days of enactment, to enter into agreements to loan Federal museum artifacts and objects from Interior agencies to the Foundation without monetary consideration, and states that no Federal entity is involved in the library's operation unless requested by the non-Federal operator. BILLS-SEL-01
